p53: 53.  The Court observes that in the present case the applicant, who is of Roma origin, complained about remarks and expressions which, in his view, debased the Roma community. While the applicant was admittedly not personally targeted, remarks concerning the ethnic group to which he belongs could offend his sensibilities. Moreover, the applicant’s standing was not challenged in the domestic proceedings, the merits of the case thus having been examined by the domestic courts at two levels of jurisdiction.
p54: 54.  In the light of the foregoing, and of the need to apply the criteria for victim status in a flexible manner, the Court accepts that the applicant, although not directly targeted by the impugned passages, can be considered a victim of the facts complained of within the meaning of Article 34 of the Convention. It therefore dismisses the Government’s preliminary objection concerning victim status.
p55: 55.  The applicant alleged that certain passages of the book entitled “The Gypsies in Turkey” contained remarks and expressions that debased the Roma community. He referred in particular to the chapter of the book in which the author described the lifestyle of Roma living in certain Turkish cities, and in particular their alleged involvement in illegal activities (see paragraph 12 above). He considered that the author’s general intention was of little importance, since in his view the passages in question in themselves constituted a clear insult to the Roma community. He therefore criticised the decisions by which the domestic courts had dismissed his claim for compensation.
p56: 56.  The Government stated that the book had been published by the Ministry of Culture on the recommendation of its Publications Advisory Board. They added that, according to that board’s report, the book was a comparative academic study, prepared with a view to contributing to ethnic research in Turkey. The study provided information on the origins, language, traditions, beliefs, festivals, cuisine, clothing, music and living conditions of the Roma community. The Government asserted that, following the applicant’s protests, the book had been re-examined by several university professors, who had found that it did not contain any insulting remarks. Lastly, the Government submitted that the Ministry of Culture devoted considerable efforts to promoting Roma culture and traditions.
p57: 57.  The Chamber held that while the passages and remarks cited by the applicant, read on their own, appeared to be discriminatory and insulting, it could not be concluded, following an examination of the book as a whole, that the author had acted in bad faith or with the intention of insulting the Roma community. The Chamber had particular regard to the conclusion of the book, in which the author clearly explained that “The Gypsies in Turkey” was an academic study based on comparative analysis and focusing on the history and socio-economic living conditions of the Roma people in Turkey. It considered that if the author had described a prejudiced portrayal of Roma, it was in order to show how that community was perceived by the public. It therefore concluded that there had been no violation of the applicant’s rights under the Convention.
p58: 58.  The Court reiterates that the notion of “private life” within the meaning of Article 8 of the Convention is a broad term not susceptible to exhaustive definition. The notion of personal autonomy is an important principle underlying the interpretation of the guarantees of that provision. It can therefore embrace multiple aspects of a person’s physical and social identity. The Court further reiterates that it has accepted in the past that an individual’s ethnic identity must be regarded as an important element of his or her private life (see S. and Marper v. the United Kingdom [GC], nos. 30562/04 and 30566/04, § 66, ECHR 2008, and Ciubotaru v. Moldova, no. 27138/04, § 49, 27 April 2010). In particular, any negative stereotyping of a group, when it reaches a certain level, is capable of impacting on the group’s sense of identity and the feelings of self-worth and self-confidence of members of the group. It is in this sense that it can be seen as affecting the private life of members of the group.
p59: 59.  Moreover, although the object of Article 8 is essentially that of protecting the individual against arbitrary interference by the public authorities, it does not merely compel the State to abstain from such interference: in addition to this negative undertaking, there may be positive obligations inherent in an effective respect for private life, which may involve the adoption of measures designed to secure respect for private life even in the sphere of the relations of individuals between themselves (see Tavlı v. Turkey, no. 11449/02, § 28, 9 November 2006, and Ciubotaru, cited above, § 50).
